claim: RSC is composed of a rigid tripartite core and two flexible lobes.
source: Here, we report cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and crosslinking mass spectrometry (CLMS) studies of yeast RSC complex and show that RSC is composed of a rigid tripartite core and two flexible lobes.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by cryo-EM structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The core structure of RSC is scaffolded by an asymmetric Rsc8 dimer.
source: The core structure is scaffolded by an asymmetric Rsc8 dimer and built with the evolutionarily conserved subunits Sfh1, Rsc6, Rsc9 and Sth1.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by structural data showing Rsc8 dimer organization.

claim: The flexible ATPase lobe is composed of helicase subunit Sth1, Arp7, Arp9 and Rtt102.
source: The flexible ATPase lobe, composed of helicase subunit Sth1, Arp7, Arp9 and Rtt102, is anchored to this core by the N-terminus of Sth1.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by structural analysis.

claim: RSC engages histones and nucleosomal DNA through one arm of the core structure, composed of the Rsc8 SWIRM domains, Sfh1 and Npl6.
source: Our cryo-EM analysis of RSC bound to a nucleosome core particle shows that in addition to the expected nucleosome-Sth1 interactions, RSC engages histones and nucleosomal DNA through one arm of the core structure, composed of the Rsc8 SWIRM domains, Sfh1 and Npl6.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by cryo-EM data of RSC-NCP complex.

claim: Eukaryotes have four major families of chromatin remodelers: SWI/SNF, ISWI, CHD, and INO80.
source: Eukaryotes have four major families of chromatin remodelers: SWI/SNF, ISWI, CHD, and INO80 (Clapier and Cairns, 2009).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In S. cerevisiae there are two members of the SWI/SNF family of chromatin remodelers: RSC and SWI/SNF.
source: In S. cerevisiae there are two members of the SWI/SNF family of chromatin remodelers: RSC and SWI/SNF (Côté et al., 1994; Cairns et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SWI/SNF chromatin remodelers reposition nucleosomes by translocating DNA around the histone octamer.
source: SWI/SNF chromatin remodelers reposition nucleosomes by translocating DNA around the histone octamer, and in vitro assays have shown that they move nucleosomes to the ends of linear DNA fragments before evicting the histones from the DNA (Clapier et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: RSC is essential for yeast viability.
source: RSC is essential for yeast viability and is ten times more abundant than SWI/SNF (Cairns et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: RSC is ten times more abundant than SWI/SNF.
source: RSC is essential for yeast viability and is ten times more abundant than SWI/SNF (Cairns et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: RSC is responsible for maintaining nucleosome free regions (NFR).
source: In the context of transcription, RSC is responsible for maintaining nucleosome free regions (NFR), while SWI/SNF plays a role in remodeling nucleosomes during transcription initiation (Nagai et al., 2017; Krietenstein et al., 2016; Klein-Brill et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SWI/SNF plays a role in remodeling nucleosomes during transcription initiation.
source: In the context of transcription, RSC is responsible for maintaining nucleosome free regions (NFR), while SWI/SNF plays a role in remodeling nucleosomes during transcription initiation (Nagai et al., 2017; Krietenstein et al., 2016; Klein-Brill et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RSC is involved in mitotic division, double stranded break repair, and telomere maintenance.
source: Additionally, RSC is also involved in many transcription-independent processes, such as mitotic division, double stranded break repair, and telomere maintenance (Krietenstein et al., 2016; Erkina et al., 2010; Kuryan et al., 2012; Campsteijn et al., 2007; Shim et al., 2007; Ungar et al., 2009; Ng et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RSC has a molecular weight of ~1.1 MDa.
source: RSC has a molecular weight of ~1.1 MDa and is composed of 17 proteins, with two copies of Rsc8 and one copy of either Rsc1 or Rsc2 (Cairns et al., 1996; Cairns et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RSC is composed of 17 proteins, with two copies of Rsc8 and one copy of either Rsc1 or Rsc2.
source: RSC has a molecular weight of ~1.1 MDa and is composed of 17 proteins, with two copies of Rsc8 and one copy of either Rsc1 or Rsc2 (Cairns et al., 1996; Cairns et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Seven proteins (Arp7, Arp9, Rsc6, Rsc8, Sfh1, Sth1 and Rsc9) are conserved in all eukaryotic SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complexes.
source: Seven of the proteins (Arp7, Arp9, Rsc6, Rsc8, Sfh1, Sth1 and Rsc9) are conserved in all eukaryotic SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complexes, with Sth1 containing the ATPase domain that is responsible for the remodeling activity (Cairns et al., 1996; Saha et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sth1 contains the ATPase domain that is responsible for the remodeling activity.
source: Seven of the proteins (Arp7, Arp9, Rsc6, Rsc8, Sfh1, Sth1 and Rsc9) are conserved in all eukaryotic SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complexes, with Sth1 containing the ATPase domain that is responsible for the remodeling activity (Cairns et al., 1996; Saha et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Arp7, Arp9 and Rtt102 are shared between RSC and SWI/SNF.
source: Three subunits, Arp7, Arp9 and Rtt102, are shared between RSC and SWI/SNF, and the two Arps have been found to be important for efficient remodeling activity of RSC (Clapier et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Arp7 and Arp9 have been found to be important for efficient remodeling activity of RSC.
source: Three subunits, Arp7, Arp9 and Rtt102, are shared between RSC and SWI/SNF, and the two Arps have been found to be important for efficient remodeling activity of RSC (Clapier et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Swi3 (the SWI/SNF paralog of Rsc8) has been shown to be important for complex assembly and to likely play a scaffolding role.
source: The SWI/SNF paralog of Rsc8, Swi3, has been shown to be important for complex assembly and to likely play a scaffolding role (Yang et al., 2007), while the paralog of Sfh1, Snf5, has been found to be important for remodeling activity (Sen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Snf5 (the paralog of Sfh1) has been found to be important for remodeling activity.
source: The SWI/SNF paralog of Rsc8, Swi3, has been shown to be important for complex assembly and to likely play a scaffolding role (Yang et al., 2007), while the paralog of Sfh1, Snf5, has been found to be important for remodeling activity (Sen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: RSC contains six bromodomains (BrDs), two in RSC1/2 and Rsc4, and one in Rsc58 and Sth1.
source: RSC contains six bromodomains (BrDs), two in RSC1/2 and Rsc4, and one in Rsc58 and Sth1.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: Rsc1/2 contain a BAH domain.
source: Additionally, Rsc1/2 also contain a BAH domain.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: The BrD and BAH domains of RSC have all been shown to interact with histones H3.
source: The BrD and BAH domains of RSC have all been shown to interact with histones H3 (Chambers et al., 2013), with the BrDs favoring acetylated H3 tails (Zhang et al., 2010), and in vitro binding assays have shown that the affinity of RSC for acetylated H3 nucleosomes is indeed greater than for unmodified nucleosomes (Chatterjee et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The BrDs of RSC favor acetylated H3 tails.
source: The BrD and BAH domains of RSC have all been shown to interact with histones H3 (Chambers et al., 2013), with the BrDs favoring acetylated H3 tails (Zhang et al., 2010), and in vitro binding assays have shown that the affinity of RSC for acetylated H3 nucleosomes is indeed greater than for unmodified nucleosomes (Chatterjee et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The affinity of RSC for acetylated H3 nucleosomes is greater than for unmodified nucleosomes.
source: The BrD and BAH domains of RSC have all been shown to interact with histones H3 (Chambers et al., 2013), with the BrDs favoring acetylated H3 tails (Zhang et al., 2010), and in vitro binding assays have shown that the affinity of RSC for acetylated H3 nucleosomes is indeed greater than for unmodified nucleosomes (Chatterjee et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In vivo deletions or mutations in BrD and BAH domains have been shown to decrease cell survival.
source: In vivo deletions or mutations in these domains have been shown to decrease cell survival (Cairns et al., 1999; Kasten et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The fungal-specific subunits Npl6, Htl1, Ldb7, Rsc3 and Rsc30 have been proposed to form a structural module.
source: The fungal-specific subunits Npl6, Htl1, Ldb7, Rsc3 and Rsc30, have been proposed to form a structural module (Wilson et al., 2006), with Npl6 and Htl1 interacting with Rsc8, and Ldb7 with Sth1 and Arp9.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Npl6 and Htl1 interact with Rsc8.
source: The fungal-specific subunits Npl6, Htl1, Ldb7, Rsc3 and Rsc30, have been proposed to form a structural module (Wilson et al., 2006), with Npl6 and Htl1 interacting with Rsc8, and Ldb7 with Sth1 and Arp9.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Ldb7 interacts with Sth1 and Arp9.
source: The fungal-specific subunits Npl6, Htl1, Ldb7, Rsc3 and Rsc30, have been proposed to form a structural module (Wilson et al., 2006), with Npl6 and Htl1 interacting with Rsc8, and Ldb7 with Sth1 and Arp9.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Rsc3 and Rsc30 dimerize with each other and share a very similar architecture.
source: Rsc3 and Rsc30, which dimerize with each other, share a very similar architecture (Angus-Hill et al., 2001), with an N-terminal Zinc cluster that has been shown to bind to the DNA sequence CGCG that preferentially occurs at gene promoters (Badis et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Rsc3 and Rsc30 have an N-terminal Zinc cluster that binds to the DNA sequence CGCG that preferentially occurs at gene promoters.
source: Rsc3 and Rsc30, which dimerize with each other, share a very similar architecture (Angus-Hill et al., 2001), with an N-terminal Zinc cluster that has been shown to bind to the DNA sequence CGCG that preferentially occurs at gene promoters (Badis et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Deletion of Rsc3 has been shown to weaken the ability of RSC to maintain NFR in vivo.
source: Deletion of Rsc3 has been shown to weaken the ability of RSC to maintain NFR in vivo (Badis et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The structure of the core of RSC was determined to ~3.0 Å resolution.
source: We determined the structure of the core to ~3.0 Å and mapped 14 proteins within this region: Rsc1/2, Rsc3, Rsc4, Rsc6, Rsc8 (two copies), Rsc9, Rsc30, Rsc58, Ldb7, Npl6, Htl1, Sfh1, and Sth1 (Figure 1B,C,F; Figure 1—figure supplements 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by cryo-EM data.

claim: 14 proteins were mapped within the core region of RSC: Rsc1/2, Rsc3, Rsc4, Rsc6, Rsc8 (two copies), Rsc9, Rsc30, Rsc58, Ldb7, Npl6, Htl1, Sfh1, and Sth1.
source: We determined the structure of the core to ~3.0 Å and mapped 14 proteins within this region: Rsc1/2, Rsc3, Rsc4, Rsc6, Rsc8 (two copies), Rsc9, Rsc30, Rsc58, Ldb7, Npl6, Htl1, Sfh1, and Sth1 (Figure 1B,C,F; Figure 1—figure supplements 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by cryo-EM data.

claim: About 90% (151/168) of mappable crosslinks in the RSC core structure are within 38 Å distance.
source: About 90% (151/168) of mappable crosslinks in our model of the RSC core structure are within 38 Å distance.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by crosslinking mass spectrometry data.

claim: A 19 Å resolution map of RSC bound to a nucleosome core particle (NCP) modified with H3K4me3 and H3K(9/14/18)ac was obtained.
source: In order to shed light on the interaction of RSC with its substrate, we also obtained a 19 Å resolution map of RSC bound to a nucleosome core particle (NCP) modified with H3K4me3 and H3K(9/14/18)ac (Figure 1D,E,F; Figure 1—figure supplement 9).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by cryo-EM data.

claim: No density for the ATPase domain of Sth1 was observed in the RSC-NCP structure.
source: We do not observe any density for the ATPase domain of Sth1; however, based on the structure of the Sth1 homolog Snf2 bound to the NCP, we expect the catalytic subunit to bind super-helical location-2 (SHL2) (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by cryo-EM data and inference from homologous structures.

claim: Two distinct modes of NCP binding by RSC were observed: one where the whole tail is swiveled towards the nucleosome (termed swiveled), and one where only a small region emanating from the tail reaches towards the NCP (termed locked).
source: Our data show two distinct modes of NCP binding by RSC, one where the whole tail is swiveled towards the nucleosome (termed swiveled), and one where only a small region emanating from the tail reaches towards the NCP (termed locked) (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by cryo-EM data.

claim: The contacts made by the RSC core with the NCP are sufficient for nucleosome engagement.
source: The fact that we observe nucleosome-bound RSC, even without a stable binding of the catalytic domain of Sth1 to the NCP, indicates that the contacts through the RSC core are sufficient for nucleosome engagement.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by inference from cryo-EM data.

claim: The contacts made by the RSC core with the NCP contribute to the processivity of the nucleosome remodeling function of the catalytic domain of Sth1.
source: We propose that the contacts made by the RSC core with the NCP contribute to the processivity of the nucleosome remodeling function of the catalytic domain of Sth1 (see below).
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a proposal based on structural observations.

claim: An asymmetric Rsc8 dimer defines the backbone for the RSC complex, scaffolding the three core lobes and contacting all core proteins except Rsc3 and Rsc30.
source: An asymmetric Rsc8 dimer defines the backbone for the complex, scaffolding the three core lobes and contacting all core proteins except Rsc3 and Rsc30 (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural data.

claim: Rsc8 has four conserved domains: SWIRM, ZZ, SANT, and coiled coil (CC).
source: Rsc8 has four conserved domains, which are, from N to C terminus: SWIRM, ZZ, SANT, and coiled coil (CC) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural data.

claim: Rsc8 homologs are critical for the integrity of their respective SWI/SNF chromatin remodelers.
source: Previous work has shown that Rsc8 homologs are critical for the integrity of their respective SWI/SNF chromatin remodelers, supporting the idea that Rsc8 and its homologs are the structural backbone for all SWI/SNF family of remodelers (Mashtalir et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The body lobe of RSC contains a helical bundle backbone, an α-solenoid belly and a β-sandwich hook.
source: The body lobe of RSC contains a helical bundle backbone, an α-solenoid belly and a β-sandwich hook (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural data.

claim: The helical bundle in the body lobe is made up of the two CC domains of Rsc8, along with the CC domains of Rsc6 and Htl1.
source: The helical bundle is made up of the two CC domains of Rsc8, along with the CC domains of Rsc6 and Htl1.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural data.

claim: The α-solenoid belly is made up of the armadillo repeats of Rsc9 and the SwiB domain of Rsc6.
source: This helical bundle interacts with the α-solenoid belly made up of the armadillo repeats of Rsc9 and the SwiB domain of Rsc6.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural data.

claim: The Rsc3 and Rsc30 dimer appears to be absent in 75% of the RSC particles that were used in the high-resolution analysis.
source: The Rsc3 and Rsc30 dimer appears to be absent in 75% of the RSC particles that were used in the high-resolution analysis (Figure 3B), in agreement with previous findings showing that some RSC complexes lack Rsc3 and Rsc30 (Angus-Hill et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by cryo-EM data and citation to previous literature.

claim: The presence or absence of the Rsc3 and Rsc30 dimer correlates with the presence or absence of most of the tail lobe.
source: During our image analysis, we found that the presence or absence of the Rsc3 and Rsc30 dimer correlates well with the presence or absence of most of the tail lobe, making the Rsc3 and Rsc30 subunits the most likely constituents of this very flexible lobe (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by cryo-EM data analysis.

claim: The arm lobe is made of the two SWIRM domains of Rsc8 held together by the Scaffold domain of Npl6 and the RPT1 and RPT2 domains of Sfh1.
source: Four proteins contribute to most of the arm lobe, which is made of the two SWIRM domains of Rsc8 held together by the Scaffold domain of Npl6 and the RPT1 and RPT2 domains of Sfh1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural data.

claim: The arm lobe makes major interactions with the nucleosome, contacting both the acidic patch and nucleosomal DNA.
source: Within our RSC-NCP structure, the arm lobe makes major interactions with the nucleosome, contacting both the acidic patch and nucleosomal DNA (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by cryo-EM data of RSC-NCP complex.

claim: The region of the arm that contacts the acidic patch appears to emanate from the C-terminal end of the RPT2 domain of Sfh1.
source: The region of the arm that contacts the acidic patch appears to emanate from the C-terminal end of the RPT2 domain of Sfh1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by cryo-EM data.

claim: The C-terminal region of Sfh1 is highly conserved and contains nine lysine and arginine residues that are predicted to form a helix.
source: This region of Sfh1 is highly conserved and contains nine lysine and arginine residues that are predicted to form a helix (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by sequence analysis and prediction.

claim: Deletion of Snf5 (SWI/SNF homolog of Sfh1) in yeast results in less efficient chromatin remodeling activity of the SWI/SNF complex.
source: The involvement of this region in nucleosome binding is supported by the fact that deletion of Snf5 (SWI/SNF homolog of Sfh1) in yeast results in less efficient chromatin remodeling activity of the SWI/SNF complex (Sen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The CRC domain of Npl6 is the likely candidate for binding the nucleosomal DNA.
source: The WH domain of SMARCB has been shown to bind DNA and would be small enough to be accommodated within the extra density observed in our RSC-NCP structure, making the CRC domain of Npl6 the likely candidate for binding the nucleosomal DNA (Figure 4B) (Allen et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by inference from structural data and citation to previous literature.

claim: Six RSC subunits contribute majorly to the head lobe: Rsc8, Rsc58, Sth1, Rsc4, and Rsc1/2.
source: Six RSC subunits contribute majorly to the head lobe of RSC, which is made of the ZZ and SANT domains of the two copies of Rsc8, the BrD and Scaffold II domain of Rsc58, the Scaffold I and part of Scaffold II domain of Sth1, the β-barrel domain of Rsc4 and the anchor domain of Rsc1/2 (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural data.

claim: Only Rsc8 and Sth1 are evolutionarily conserved among the subunits contributing to the head lobe.
source: Of these proteins, only Rsc8 and Sth1 are evolutionarily conserved, suggesting that this region probably contributes to specific functions of the RSC complex.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by evolutionary analysis.

claim: Rsc58, Rsc4 and Rsc1/2 contain histone reader domains: BrD and BAH domains.
source: Rsc58, Rsc4 and Rsc1/2 are notable for containing histone reader domains: BrD and BAH domains.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by domain analysis.

claim: BrD and BAH domains have been shown to interact with acetylated lysines on histone tails, particularly H3.
source: These domains have been shown to interact with acetylated lysines on histone tails, particularly H3 (Chambers et al., 2013; Chatterjee et al., 2011; Duan and Smerdon, 2014).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Only the BrD of Rsc58 could be modeled in the structure.
source: We could only model the BrD of Rsc58, while the remaining BrDs and the BAH domain extend from flexible linkers and are not visible in our structure (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural data.

claim: The BrD-containing subunits in the RSC-nucleosome model are positioned so that these domains could reach the H3 tails of the engaged nucleosome.
source: Based on the position of the head relative to the arm lobe, the BrD-containing subunits in our RSC-nucleosome model are positioned so that these domains could reach the H3 tails of the engaged nucleosome (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural modeling.

claim: Different bromodomains within RSC can recognize different acetylation sites.
source: Microarray data have shown that different bromodomains within RSC can recognize different acetylation sites, which could allow the complex to be targeted to a wide variety of genomic loci (Zhang et al., 2010; Filippakopoulos et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The yeast SWI/SNF and its human homolog BAF have just one BrD – on the ATPase subunit.
source: The yeast SWI/SNF and its human homolog BAF have just one BrD – on the ATPase subunit – while human PBAF has eight, indicating that these domains may contribute to functional specificity of different classes within the SWI/SNF family.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by knowledge of complex composition.

claim: Human PBAF has eight BrDs.
source: The yeast SWI/SNF and its human homolog BAF have just one BrD – on the ATPase subunit – while human PBAF has eight, indicating that these domains may contribute to functional specificity of different classes within the SWI/SNF family.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by knowledge of complex composition.

claim: Initial recruitment of RSC to a nucleosome likely occurs through interaction with H3 acetylation marks.
source: Initial recruitment of RSC to a nucleosome likely occurs through interaction with H3 acetylation marks, given that RSC has an increased affinity for these nucleosomes (Kasten et al., 2004) and that most of them as flexible, facilitating an initial encounter.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a proposal based on structural observations and citation to previous literature.

claim: RSC can engage the nucleosome through its arm region and place the SHL2 site of the nucleosome in position to bind the flexibly tethered catalytic domain of Sth1.
source: RSC could then engage the nucleosome through its arm region and place the SHL2 site of the nucleosome in position to bind the flexibly tethered catalytic domain of Sth1.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a proposal based on structural observations.

claim: The ATPase domain of Sth1 translocates the DNA around the histone octamer while the core of RSC holds onto the histone core through its direct interactions with histones.
source: The ATPase domain would then be able to translocate the DNA around the histone octamer, while the core of RSC holds onto the histone core through its direct interactions with histones.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a proposal based on structural observations.

claim: All SWI/SNF complexes have bromodomains to bind acetylated histones.
source: Specifically, all complexes have bromodomains to bind acetylated histones (minimally in the C-terminus of their catalytic subunit), a Sfh1 homolog to bind the acidic patch of the nucleosome, and a catalytic DNA translocase domain to remodel nucleosomes (Figure 2—source data 1) (Clapier and Cairns, 2009).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by knowledge and citation.

claim: All SWI/SNF complexes have a Sfh1 homolog to bind the acidic patch of the nucleosome.
source: Specifically, all complexes have bromodomains to bind acetylated histones (minimally in the C-terminus of their catalytic subunit), a Sfh1 homolog to bind the acidic patch of the nucleosome, and a catalytic DNA translocase domain to remodel nucleosomes (Figure 2—source data 1) (Clapier and Cairns, 2009).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by knowledge and citation.

claim: All SWI/SNF complexes have a catalytic DNA translocase domain to remodel nucleosomes.
source: Specifically, all complexes have bromodomains to bind acetylated histones (minimally in the C-terminus of their catalytic subunit), a Sfh1 homolog to bind the acidic patch of the nucleosome, and a catalytic DNA translocase domain to remodel nucleosomes (Figure 2—source data 1) (Clapier and Cairns, 2009).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by knowledge and citation.

claim: Dimerization of the Rsc8 CC domains is most likely the first step in RSC complex assembly.
source: According to this analysis, dimerization of the Rsc8 CC domains is most likely the first step in RSC complex assembly, followed by the binding of Rsc6 to this CC dimer.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an inference based on structural analysis and comparison to mammalian complexes.

claim: The binding of Rsc6 to the Rsc8 CC dimer follows the dimerization of Rsc8 CC domains in RSC assembly.
source: According to this analysis, dimerization of the Rsc8 CC domains is most likely the first step in RSC complex assembly, followed by the binding of Rsc6 to this CC dimer.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: The RPT1 and RPT2 motifs within Sfh1 bring the two SWIRM domains of Rsc8 together.
source: The RPT1 and RPT2 motifs within Sfh1 would then bring the two SWIRM domains of Rsc8 together.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: Initial dimerization of SMARCC (the mammalian Rsc8 homolog) is followed by the sequential binding of SMARCD, SMARCB, and SMARCE to form the BAF core.
source: This initial order of assembly is based on the assembly intermediates identified for the mammalian SWI/SNF complexes BAF and PBAF (Mashtalir et al., 2018) where initial dimerization of SMARCC (the mammalian Rsc8 homolog) is followed by the sequential binding of SMARCD (the mammalian Rsc6 homolog), SMARCB (the mammalian Sfh1 homolog), and SMARCE (no known RSC/yeast homolog) to form the BAF core.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The armadillo repeat domain of Rsc9 binds the Rsc8 CC and Rsc6 to form most of the body lobe.
source: The armadillo repeat domain of Rsc9 binds the Rsc8 CC and Rsc6 to form most of the body lobe, while the scaffolding domains (I and II) of Sth1 contribute to both the head and body regions and exit towards the flexible leg lobe.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural data.

claim: The scaffolding domains (I and II) of Sth1 contribute to both the head and body regions and exit towards the flexible leg lobe.
source: The armadillo repeat domain of Rsc9 binds the Rsc8 CC and Rsc6 to form most of the body lobe, while the scaffolding domains (I and II) of Sth1 contribute to both the head and body regions and exit towards the flexible leg lobe.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural data.

claim: The integration of Sth1 into the complex leads to recruitment of the components of the ARP module (Arp7, Arp9 and Rtt102).
source: The integration of Sth1 into the complex would also lead to recruitment of the components of the ARP module (Arp7, Arp9 and Rtt102).
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: The initial assembly process of RSC primarily involves evolutionarily conserved subunits and domains and is thus likely conserved for all SWI/SNF chromatin remodelers.
source: It is important to note that this initial assembly process primarily involves evolutionarily conserved subunits and domains and is thus likely conserved for all SWI/SNF chromatin remodelers (Kadoch and Crabtree, 2015).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by inference and citation.

claim: The structural similarities between yeast SWI/SNF and RSC complexes support the proposed assembly model.
source: This model is supported by the structural similarities we observe between the yeast SWI/SNF and RSC complexes (and in agreement with a recently reported structure of yeast SWI/SNF bound to a nucleosome by Han et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural comparison and citation.

claim: RSC assembly continues with the addition of the yeast specific factor Npl6, which completes the arm lobe.
source: In the case of RSC, assembly would then continue with the addition of the yeast specific factor Npl6, which completes the arm lobe, and RSC-specific subunits Htl1, Rsc58, Rsc1/2, Rsc4, and Ldb7.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: The last two subunits to be recruited to the RSC complex are likely the RSC-specific subunits Rsc3 and Rsc30, which form the tail module.
source: The last two subunits to be recruited to the complex are likely the RSC-specific subunits Rsc3 and Rsc30, which form the tail module.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: RSC is composed of five main lobes: three that form a relatively rigid core (head, body and arm) and two that are flexibly attached (leg and tail).
source: We found that RSC is composed of five main lobes, three that form a relatively rigid core (head, body and arm) and two that are flexibly attached (leg and tail) (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Yeast SWI/SNF has a rigid core sharing some similar features with RSC and a flexible leg that occupies similar overall positions.
source: Our negative stain analysis of the yeast SWI/SNF complex shows that, like RSC, it has a rigid core sharing some similar features, and a flexible leg that occupies similar overall positions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by negative stain EM data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: SWI/SNF lacks a tail lobe, indicating that while RSC and SWI/SNF share a conserved core architecture, RSC features additional regulatory domains.
source: However, SWI/SNF lacks a tail lobe, indicating that while RSC and SWI/SNF share a conserved core architecture, RSC features additional regulatory domains (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by comparison of structures shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 780 unique inter-molecular links between different subunits and 617 unique intra-molecular links within the same subunits were identified by crosslinking mass spectrometry.
source: We identified 780 unique inter-molecular links between different subunits and 617 unique intra-molecular links within the same subunits.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by crosslinking mass spectrometry data.

claim: The core of RSC binds the nucleosome in a well-defined orientation that places the catalytic domain of Sth1 in a position that would allow it to interact with the SHL2.
source: Altogether, the core of RSC appears to bind the nucleosome in a well-defined orientation that in our docking-based model places the catalytic domain of Sth1 in a position that would allow it to interact with the SHL2.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural modeling.

claim: The RSC-NCP structure is a likely intermediate in a pathway to full engagement of a nucleosome by RSC.
source: It also makes our structure a likely intermediate in a pathway to full engagement of a nucleosome by RSC.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an inference based on structural observations.

claim: Five of the proteins defining the RSC core (Rsc8, Rsc6, Rsc9, Sth1, and Sfh1) are evolutionarily conserved throughout the eukaryotic SWI/SNF family and comprise 72% of the mass of the core density.
source: Five of these proteins (Rsc8, Rsc6, Rsc9, Sth1, and Sfh1) are evolutionarily conserved throughout the eukaryotic SWI/SNF family, and comprise 72% of the mass of the core density (Figure 2A; Figure 2—source data 1) (Wang et al., 1996; Kadoch and Crabtree, 2015).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural data and citations.

claim: The SWIRM domains of Rsc8 are in the arm lobe.
source: The SWIRM domains are in the arm, the ZZ and SANT domains in the head and the CC domains in the body.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural data.

claim: The ZZ and SANT domains of Rsc8 are in the head lobe.
source: The SWIRM domains are in the arm, the ZZ and SANT domains in the head and the CC domains in the body.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural data.

claim: The CC domains of Rsc8 are in the body lobe.
source: The SWIRM domains are in the arm, the ZZ and SANT domains in the head and the CC domains in the body.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural data.

claim: Most of the structured regions of Rsc6 are in the body lobe, except for a small region at the very C-terminus (residues 445–483).
source: Most of the structured regions of Rsc6 are in the body, except for a small region at the very C-terminus of the protein (residues 445–483), which occupies the space in between the three lobes.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural data.

claim: Rsc9 is primarily located in the body lobe, but a small region at the very N-terminus (residues 28–80) interacts with the surface of the arm and head lobes.
source: Rsc9 also primarily located in the body, but for a small region at the very N-terminus terminus (residues 28–80) interacts with the surface of the arm and head lobes.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural data.

claim: The N-terminal BrD and C-terminal Scaffold II domain of Rsc58 are in the head lobe, while the central Scaffold I domain is in the body lobe.
source: The N-terminal BrD and C-terminal Scaffold II domain of Rsc58 are in the head lobe, while the central Scaffold I domain is in the body lobe.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural data.

claim: Sth1 spans three lobes: the head, body and leg.
source: Sth1 spans three lobes, the head, body and leg.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural data.

claim: The Scaffold I domain of Sth1 is in the head lobe.
source: The Scaffold I domain is in the head while the Scaffold II domain goes between the body to the head and back to the body.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural data.

claim: The Scaffold II domain of Sth1 goes between the body to the head and back to the body.
source: The Scaffold I domain is in the head while the Scaffold II domain goes between the body to the head and back to the body.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural data.

claim: Sth1 continues from the Scaffold II domain to the HSA helix that, along with Arp7, Arp9 and Rtt102, form the leg lobe.
source: From the RSC-NCP model, we observe that Sth1 then continues from the Scaffold II domain to the HSA helix that, along with Arp7, Arp9 and Rtt102, form the leg lobe (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural modeling shown in Figure 2D.

claim: From the HSA helix, Sth1 continues into the ATPase domain that would putatively bind the nucleosome at position SHL2.
source: From the HSA helix, Sth1 continues into the ATPase domain that would putatively bind the nucleosome at position SHL2 (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural modeling shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The hook region off the belly of the body lobe contains β-strands from Rsc9 and Rsc6 that come together to form a β-sandwich.
source: Finally, the hook region off the belly contains β-strands from Rsc9 and Rsc6 that come to together to form a b-sandwich.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural data.

claim: The RFX-type WH of Rsc9 is likely part of the tail.
source: Given the position of the Rsc9 sequences model in our structure, it is likely that the RFX-type WH of Rsc9 is part of the tail.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as an inference based on structural data.

claim: A segment of Rsc58 binds between the belly and the backbone of the body lobe.
source: These include a segment of Rsc58 that binds between the belly and the backbone, a small segment of Sth1 that binds to the surface of the helical bundle, and a small segment of Sth1 that binds the surface of the armadillo repeat (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The Rsc3 and Rsc30 dimer binds the surface of the Rsc9 armadillo repeat on top of Sth1.
source: The last two components of the body are the Rsc3 and Rsc30 dimer that binds the surface of the Rsc9 armadillo repeat on top of Sth1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by structural data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Some RSC complexes lack Rsc3 and Rsc30.
source: The Rsc3 and Rsc30 dimer appears to be absent in 75% of the RSC particles that were used in the high-resolution analysis (Figure 3B), in agreement with previous findings showing that some RSC complexes lack Rsc3 and Rsc30 (Angus-Hill et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Rsc3 and Rsc30 subunits are the most likely constituents of the very flexible tail lobe.
source: During our image analysis, we found that the presence or absence of the Rsc3 and Rsc30 dimer correlates well with the presence or absence of most of the tail lobe, making the Rsc3 and Rsc30 subunits the most likely constituents of this very flexible lobe (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by cryo-EM data analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There are no equivalent subunits to Rsc3 and Rsc30 in the yeast SWI-SNF complex.
source: The fact that there are no equivalent subunits in the yeast SWI-SNF complex, for which the tail domain is missing, further supports this assignment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.
